blocks.x: You don't have any middle name, huh?
No, no other name.
And your name? Yeah, and my name is Dick Allen, and we're at 1002 Valette Street in Algiers, and today is, what's today's date? It's March the, you know today's date?
No, I can tell you in a minute, though.

No, no, wait a minute. I got it on my watch. It's March the 24th, 1972. Uh, I guess the first thing you do is to begin at the beginning. You have to tell us about when you were born and where, your family and all that?
Yeah, well, uh, I was born December the 14th, 1897.
Mm-hmm. 1897.
I'll be 74, 74 years of age now. Mm-hmm. This coming December, I'll be 75. I see.
Where, where were you born? Born here in Algiers.
On Brooklyn or on, uh? In the all my life, right here. Siglin Street. Yeah, S-E-G-U-I-N. Mm-hmm. You know the number?
I know that was around in about, uh... Let's see if it's a term. That was around about the 400 block. Yeah, I see.
I see.
I see. I see. Where, where were you born?
I see. Where, where were you born?
Yeah, but what street?
Uh...
What street were you born on?
I was born on Siglin Street.
Siglin Street.
Yeah, S-E-G-U-I-N.
Mm-hmm. You know the number?
I know that was around in about, uh... Let's see if it's a term. That was around about the 400 block.
Mm-hmm. Your family lived there?
Yeah, my family lived there. Mm-hmm.
And was your father a musician?

Well, my father was a boat builder. He, uh... built boats. Mm-hmm. Of course he... My father played a little music too at the time, but his... Most of his work was boat building. He built boats. Mm-hmm. What was his name? Yeah. His name was John Bocage. Mm-hmm. And did, uh...
What about his brothers? Did they play music?
Well, no. All his brothers are dead out. He had one brother named Paul, and another brother named Feast. Well, they all dead. My father and all of them died out. Feast, his name was?
Yeah.
Do you know how you spell that?
Feast, Bocage.
Do you know how to spell it?
Oh, how? Do you know how to spell it? I don't know how to spell Feast.
Feast? F-E-I-C-E. That's the only way I know how to spell it.
Yeah. Yeah. Well, I just never had heard the name, you know. I suppose it's a French name. Must be French.
Yeah, it was all French. You see, my father... Mm-hmm. Otherwise, my grandfather came from France.
Mm-hmm.
And my daddy, he brought my daddy over here as a kid.
Mm-hmm.
Because, uh, when my boy went into the service, uh, they had a street in France by the name of the Bocage.
Oh, really?
Yeah. They named the street over there after.
Do you speak French?
Yeah.
Yourself?
Who, me?
Do you talk any French?

No, I never talked it. My father and all of them talked it, but I used to laugh at them. In other words, I was foolish not to learn it, because they used to all talk it and I'd laugh. My mother could talk it, my father could talk it, but I never did bother but learn it.
Well, did you have any other musicians in the family other than your daddy?
Huh?
Who were some of the other musicians in your family other than your daddy?
Well, they had, uh, Peter, Charlie, Henry, and my little brother Wilkins. Mm-hmm.
And, uh, what instruments did they play, like your daddy? What instruments did he play?
My daddy played guitar.
Mm-hmm.
Peter, he played, well, Peter was more of a professor, like, he played three, four different instruments. Mm-hmm. He was a trumpet man, he led fighter form, he played trombone, led piano.
Mm-hmm.
He was all around.
What, what is your relation to Pete? Uh, how are you related to Pete? Pete's cousin, first cousin. Pete, Pete and Charlie and Henry are your cousins?
Yeah. Well, Pete and, uh, Pete and Piro and them come up together. After Piro died out, well, Pete, he found the Creole Serenators.
Mm-hmm.

Of course, they went to New York. They had a couple of records that day, and they came on back and just stopped playing that, uh, out at Tranchinas, out at the lake. And they used, uh, broadcast every day on the, on the radio. Well, they had, that time they had, they had Peter, Cantrell playing drum, Laurie Warnick playing saxophone, Henry playing bass tuba, Charlie was playing Berenville. Mm-hmm.

What radio station, go ahead. Let's talk to you a while, let's see if it's working. It only took us twenty seconds, uh, then to, we cleaned the machine. We just cleaned it, so, uh. Oh, I see. Yeah, what radio station were they on? Huh? What radio station were they on? You say Pete was on the radio?
Well, I believe it was WDSU, I believe they used to come over. Mm-hmm. At that time, yeah, I think it was WDSU. Oh, yeah. Yeah, they used to come on.
We ought to go by that sometime. Yeah. And see the people that worked there. I know several people that worked there. Well, anyway, uh, back to you, to yourself. How did you get started in music?
Well, Sue this kid here, Red Allen, me and him used to be an old friend. So, I kept that thing back there for a souvenir. That was the first, first old guitar we bought for five dollars.
A cellar, huh?

Yeah. On Radford Street. A cellar. And, uh, so we used to, I used to go by his house and he'd take his trumpet and I'd take the old guitar and we'd start playing behind King Oliver records and things like that, you know.
Oh, how old were you then? And, uh. Who? How old were you then?

Who? Me? Yeah. About that time? Oh, I guess I was around about twenty-twenty-one or something like that. And, uh, well, otherwise we come as to learn that I'd play a couple of numbers like that and we picked up on little John Casney. Mm-hmm.
Clarinet player.
Probably you might have heard talk of him. He's dead now.
I knew him.
And, uh, well we picked up on little John Casney and me, Red Island, John Casney, old man Albert Glenny, Fred Bess. Well, we all got together and made a little seven piece band.
Mm-hmm.
And we started playing off, uh, little dances and things like that. Who played guitar? Well, after, uh, after Red Island, left and went to New York, I took up with Kit Thomas.
Mm-hmm. Well, tell me about the band with Red Island. What were you playing?
I was playing guitar with Red Island. Yeah. And who else did you have?
You had Glenny?

Then I played in the, uh, I played with his daddy. I played in the brass band. I played bass drum with his daddy in the brass band. Mm-hmm. And after I left his daddy, I started playing with the Excelsior Brass Band. Started playing bass drum with the Excelsior Brass Band. Mm-hmm. Well, my cousin Peter was leader of the Excelsior Brass Band at that time. Mm-hmm. And they had, uh, Peter on trumpet, George McCullen on trumpet, Charlie Love on trumpet, and Percy, Percy Umphrey. Willie Umphrey on clarinet. Uh, trombone, we had a fellow named Buddy Johnson and Harrison Bones. And, uh, another fellow playing bass trubber at that time was named, uh, Eddie Jackson. Eddie Jackson died. Mm-hmm. Well, we taken Henry. Henry played bass trubber. Well, they taken Henry in the band. It makes sense for our band at that time.
Henry is kin to you, too, now.
Uh-huh.
What kin is Henry to you, huh?
First cousins.
He's first cousin also.
Yeah, Peter first cousin and Henry first cousin. Peter and Henry's brothers. Peter, Henry, and Charlie's brothers. Mm-hmm. Go Charlie dead, Peter dead, but Henry live, and Henry's in Oakland.
Mm-hmm. Did you have alto horns in those bands?
Uh-huh.
Did you have an alto horn?
A peck horn? Who? Well, he had a bass trubber.
Yeah, but in the Excelsior, did they have baritone?
Yeah, yeah, they had peck horn. Old man Pian played peck horn, and Georgia Hooker played, uh, baritone. Mm-hmm.
Was he any kin to Joe Pian? For me?

No, I was in no relation to him. He just friendly, knowed me. Yeah. And, uh, I come to go with the Excelsior band for playing with old man Allen. Mm-hmm. They had three bands out one day playing the funeral. And I was playing with old man Allen that day. And they heard me playing the drum. So my cousin Peter then got me with the Excelsior. So I started playing with the Excelsior band until I got tired. And I quit and Henry Martin took over. Then they had come out and played. Well, Henry Martin played with them a long time until the Excelsior practically almost bust up.
Who was the snare drummer then?
Uh?
Who was the snare drummer?
Uh, Remus Matthews.
Oh, yeah. Happy.

Yeah. Well, they had three Matthews boys at that time. Used to be Bill played, Trumbo. Remus played snare drum. And his brothers, one called Turk, he used to play. Traps and snare drum, too, in the band.
Well, who was Bebe Matthews? Which one was Bebe?
Bebe, that's the one that played, uh, played trap drums.
Oh, that's, that's the same as Turk.
Yeah. That's it. Right around the corner.
Yeah. On, uh, Opelousas or?
On Newton's street, yeah.
On Newton.
Yeah, right in the back of me over there. Oh, yeah. Yeah.
Yeah, I used to hear Bebe, uh, I mean, I used to hear Remus in church. Huh? I used to hear Remus in church, in that sanctified church.

Well, Remus, Remus never, Remus always played. Yeah. The snare drum in the brass band. Yeah. He never played in the orchestra or nothing. Mm-hmm. But he was a good snare drum player in the brass band. Yeah.
Well, he was good in church. Yeah. He was playing bass drum in church.

Well, yeah, we played, he played in church. He, Remus, after that, Remus got out of the, they all retired out of the band, Remus did, and, Remus, he came after going back to church. And, um, well, he'd take my heart attack too, and he died out. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm.
Bebe died. Bill died. Yeah. All them fellas practically died out, all them old timers. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm. We never did get all the different people in Red Allen's band.
In Allen's band?
Yeah, in Red Allen, in Sonny Allen's band.
Oh, well, at the time when they, when I was with Red Allen, they had, had Red Allen, they had John Casmy, myself, old man Glenny, and a fella by the name of Lucci used to play trombone. What?
Lucci. You know, Tom Albert's son, Albert Jackson, Pinky's father? Yeah, he had a son play trombone too.
Yeah, Pinky. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah, that's right. I knew him and Tom Albert too.
Tom Albert was Lucci's father. That's right.
That's, uh, that's a, what you call him, some old man, what you call him there, he died out to, uh, Tom Albert. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah, that's Tom Albert's son. Yeah.
Yeah, Lucci, Lucci used to play around, I used to see him. He played trombone? Yeah, he used to play with John Casmy. Yeah.
Who, who played drums with Red Allen then? Welner.
Huh? Who played drums? Well, with Red Allen, with Sonny Allen. Well, at the time when we was planned to be a little boy called Johnny Thomas used to play a drum with us. Uh-huh.
And what about, uh, did you ever know a guy named R.T. Mitchell?
Fatis? No, I.T.
R.T.
Yeah, Mitchell.
No, I.T. He was a cousin of Santa for Mitchell.
No.
You didn't know Santa for Mitchell? No.
No.
He was a bass player. He was a bass player?
Yeah, he used to play with John Casmy.
I thought you'd know him.
No, he must have played with John after John left West properly. Uh-huh.
You see? Oh, John didn't stay with the band? How long was John in the band?
Well, John stayed with the band until Allen went off. Like I said, you see, when Allen first left, yeah, Allen met with King Oliver, you see,
Oliver's sentence for him. He was on the boat at the time.

Yeah. And, uh, so he asked me, uh, what did you say? He was a bass player? Yeah. He was a bass player. He was a bass player. Yeah. He was a bass player. Yeah. He was a bass player. Yeah. He was a bass player. Yeah. He was a bass player. Yeah.
Yeah.

And, uh, so he asked me, what must he do? I told him, I said, well, you young. That time Allen was young, I told him, I said, you can go on up, cause you can make it. Cause he was a bass player, a bass player. He was a bass player. And he didn't know nothing else but jazz.
Uh-huh.

Yeah. So, well, finally, he went up and he wrote me, asked me if I wanted to come up. But I told him, no, at that time I was playing by head and that fella's up there, it would make me shame about him when I tell him. So I told him, no, I didn't want to come up there. So, that's where I started playing with Thomas. Well, I played with Thomas about, oh, a couple of years I fooled around with Thomas. And I just got tired and give it up altogether. Just stop, stop playing. When did you stop? What year would that be? Oh, that'd been over around about 20 years back, I guess, when I stopped playing.
Well, you must have played with somebody after you played with Thomas, huh? Who, with Thomas?
Yeah, after Thomas.
After Thomas?
No, after Thomas I didn't play with anyone anymore.
You didn't even play with Pete?
No, I just, I played with Pete in the brass band, but I never played in the orchestra with Pete.
Well, I saw something in that book about you, is that true?
Yeah, well, in that book, yeah, that was when I played with the brass band with him.
Oh, it said you played at the Buzzards Hall with him. You never played at the Buzzards Hall?

I played one or two little dances like that, but I didn't play regularly with him, you know. Oh, I see. I even played with Professor Mineta, me, Professor Mineta and Bill Mathias, Tuyk. Yeah, I had a little line up one time and I played with them.
Oh yeah, where was that?
Oh, that was way back in, way back in about 20 years ago, that was when there was all, all them boys was living. Mm-hmm.
See?
Now, I learned how to play bass drum on the Cantrell.
You standing on the Cantrell?

Yeah, Cantrell was the snare drum player with the Excelsis, see? Mm-hmm. Every time he'd, he'd give me the signal with that, with his stick that made me know how to hit that drum. Mm-hmm. You see? And I'd like to have to play bass drum that way, on the Cantrell.
Did he teach you to read music at all? No.
Mm-mm.
You didn't have to do that, no.
Not in the band, brass band, he didn't have to read no music, and not playing those bass drum.
Mm-hmm.

In fact, I never did read no music playing this. Playing the guitar, playing by head. Mm-hmm. In fact, most of those fellas in them days, most all of them, played by head. You take little George Lewis, great clown that player, but he played by head.
Mm-hmm.
You take, uh, the majority of them fellas like, uh, Chris Kelly and all those fellas in them days, most of them fellas was no kind of a readers.
Mm-hmm.

They had very few readers in them days, but they all played nothing but that jazz by head. Of course, Peter here, Peter and Professor Minetta there, well, they, they came up in schooling, you understand? They had a schooling for, for music. See, Pete played any kind of instrument. It's likewise with Minetta. See, Minetta never done anything in his life but that. Peter, too. Peter never, never knows what a hard-to-earth work was in his life. That's all he done for a living. What you taking my time when we went out there and made seven dollars from eight to four, or eight to two o'clock in the morning, we had to make a big salary. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Otherwise, I was, I got a kick out of it just to be out there. Otherwise, tell you about the facts about it. Just so I was out there playing. I didn't care if we was out there playing and drinking and intermission. We'd have our lunch and everything like that. Well, I just got a kick out of it, me.
Well, you like to listen to bands, too, huh?
Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah.
Did you own many records? Did you own many records?

No, I didn't make, we made, me and Alan made a record, one record in my life with Sensation Rage. We made that in a house. We closed the house up and put a blank record on. We made that record. But outside of that, I never made no records anymore.
What happened to the record?
Huh?
What happened to the record?
Oh, wait, I'll be done away with it. Broke it up. Broke it up.
Well, that would be a kick to hear that.
Yeah, I wish you had a comfort, though. Yeah. Yeah, we broke it up.
Well, you like King Oliver, then? You listen to King Oliver?

Yeah, we used to have King Oliver at that time was making records, you understand? And that's how we used to learn how to play about getting King Oliver's records. Put them on the box and we'd play behind them records.
There's one of those fool motorcycles outside. I couldn't hear what you were saying.
Yeah, I say we used to get King Oliver's records, you know? Oh, yeah. Put it on the box and we'd play behind them records.
I see.
Well, that's the way this boy, you might know him, play with Thomas. Now I play bass. They call him Twat.
Oh, yeah.
I know him well. Well, Twat never had no teaching on no bass or nothing. He just picked that up, too, like, picked up that bass fiddle like that and put the records on and played behind that.
Well, is he from this neighborhood?
Uh-huh.
Does he live around here, Twat?
Who, Twat?
Yeah, Joseph Butler.

Yeah, I played with Twat. Twat used to play with him. When I was with Thomas, Twat was with him. Yeah, Twat, then, that's with Thomas a pretty good while now. Thomas comes by here now sometime. He come here and sit down, me and him talk over the old times. Sometime he want me to come over there, come down there where they play him at, round on Bourbon Street sometime. I tell him, one of these nights I'm going to come down there, you know?
Well, you have to come see me when you do that.
Yeah. Where you at, Twat?
I live in the French Quarter.
You live in the French Quarter?
I live in the 900 block of Royal.
Yeah.
I'm in the phone book.
Yeah.
He lives a block away from me.
Yeah.
And then you have to come up and see where I work, up by Tulane.
Yeah, okay.
At the university. You can hear all the Red Island, not all of them, but we've got some Red Island records up there. Yeah, I see. Yeah. But how old were you when you took up the guitar?
Oh, I was young. I was around about 19, 20 years old, something like that.
How old were you before you stopped wearing knickers and put on long pants in those days?
How long was I playing before I put on long pants?
Yeah.
Oh, well, I had on long pants. Yeah, you had on long pants.
Yeah.
When Red Island did, he had on low short pants.
Yeah.

Because one night, we played at the Corporate's Hall. And when they asked where the trumpet player was, I told him, I said, there he is. So the man said, I hide no cheering down here, you know. So I said, you're already playing. Wait till you start playing. So at that time, I started playing. At 10 o'clock, the hall was cracked down. So he asked me, he said, where you got that boy from? I said, that boy came from across the river. You know, I said, well, let me go out there. I can't be playing some trumpet up there. Well, at that time, we was playing at the Corporate's. And Sam Morgan and them was playing around at Sound of Silver. Well, we closed them up. So they came around about 10 o'clock, and they sat in. They came around and sat in for a while with us, and they played a couple of numbers, you see. They had a fellow go around and they sat in like that, you know.
Which Sam Morgan band was that? Was that the first one or the second one?
Well, they had, at that time, let's see, he had Sam, his brother Isaiah, and they had Andrew.
And Jim Crow?
Yeah, Jim Crow was with them. That's right. That's the second band, isn't it? Yeah.
Not the one with Yank.
Well, he had a, other boys, he had a, Jim Crow was with them. Jim Crow used to play banjo before he started playing trombone, you know.
I knew he played guitar. I didn't know he played banjo.
Yeah, he used to play banjo.
Oh, yeah?
And, well, then Jim Crow started playing the trombone after that, you see. But he played with Sam Morgan a long while.
Oh, I know.
Yeah, Jim Crow did.
But that was a late band.
Yeah.
That was a late band, not the one with Yank, huh?

Oh, no, that was the old-time band. Oh? Yeah, yeah, he was with them a long while. And he had another young brother there by the name of Albert, I believe, to play bass fiddle. He left away from the yard. I don't know, he's up around California there, I believe, somewhere out around that area. He never did come back this way.
But how old were you before you put on long pants?
Oh, I was guessing I was around about 17, 18 years old. Yeah.
So Sonny Allen could have had a good age on him.
Who, Allen?
Yeah, before he put on long pants. He'd be in short pants until he was 15, 16.

Well, Allen was around about, at the time Allen put on long pants, he was around about 17, 18 years old. Yeah. He used to, I'm the one who bought the pair of pants for him because I got tired of people talking about him in short pants. So I went and bought him a little long pants and put on him. So when we'd go out to play like that, he'd have long pants to put on. Yeah, he was a great, he was a great trumpet player, that boy was. But every time he came down, y'all know, from New York, he would always come here. Oh, yeah. Always come here and see me. Always throw me some money or something at the counter like that before he'd go back.
What about, uh, his mother's not alive, huh?
No, his mother died here, uh, a deep, uh, I don't tell you where, uh, she was in the crazy house.
I didn't know. What about his aunt?
His aunt, she lived down the street, sir.
I'd like to meet her. I wonder what happened to all this music, you know?
Huh?
I wonder what happened to old man Allen's music.

Now, I don't know here. I don't know what Ray had done with that music, but old man Allen had all that music stacked up back by his house. He had a house back there. And the old man had a bass drum, he had something, he had all that music stacked up there. I don't know what the boy ever done with it, you know? Well, he came down here and sold that place.
Mm-hmm.
And I, uh, I don't even know what he done with the bass drum. Because his dad had kept the bass drum, because he had his name on the bass drum, the Allen's first band, you see?
I remember it.

Yeah, and, uh, the old man kept that, but I don't know what the boy had done with it. Because Henry left his bass tuba with old man Allen, and I don't know what old man Allen done with Henry's bass tuba.
You know, what Ray and I talked about, I got a little drunk one night in New York, and I called up Ray and we were going to reorganize the Louis Russell band.
I see.
We were going to get everybody together.
Together, yeah.
And he said he still had some of the arrangements. That would have been great, you know? Yeah. Together, we could have done it then.
This old man had some nice marches back there, and I knew at that time, because that old man used to turn off and get his music. He used to have first-class marches. Yeah.
We could have... Yeah, go ahead.
The old man couldn't ever play nothing about head, but he was a good reader, the old man. He could read, but he couldn't play nothing about head.
Did you ever hear him play, Yes, Lord, I'm Cripple?
Huh? Did you ever hear him play,
Yes, Lord, I'm Cripple?
Oh, yeah.
You like that number?
Yeah.
Could he play that one by head?
Yeah. Yeah, maybe he could play that one by head.
What about Home Sweet Home?
Oh, well, he didn't bother about that.
Not those hard numbers, huh?

Well, you see, when we was in there being red, by the time the old man wanted to play some of them marches, they'd not look at red and back to him as red would blow off on something else. See, red started playing the jazz number, and the old man couldn't get in, because he couldn't.
He fixed him.

Yeah. Well, that was the way where they take the Excelsior, now the Excelsior brass band, they had some beautiful marches, and, well, Peter sometime would be playing a tune in or something. Well, Peter would get out the band, and coming back, second line, if you call him, coming on back from the graveyard, Peter would get out, because he knew he had to go play. Well, Charlie Love would take over. Well, Willie Ompford said, if you asked him now, Pete didn't lie all that. Yeah. See? And God dang it, they'd knock off hard society, and Willie put that clarinet up there, and God dang it, you could hear him from the next corner's house. Yeah.
Hear him over to where?
Could hear him from the other way down the next corner with that clarinet.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah, Willie was a strong man, on the play. John Cappie was strong going clarinet, too.
The squealer.
Yeah.
He could hear me squeal.
Hmm?
He could squeal.

Yeah, he could squeal. Yeah, he squeal like I don't know what with that clarinet. Yeah. He used to make me laugh with a lady up in Kenna. They called her Miss Cus, which they go play for on Saturday night. So, John would come in and say, Miss Cus, she said, what is it, John? I said, you got any raw eggs? She said, yeah, John. I said, give me two. John would take two of them raw eggs, and he'd suck them down, and he'd tell those red olives, and I'm going to blow you off the bandstand for the night. I don't know.
He'd suck the raw eggs, then.
I only had two brothers who were good musicians, too. One was a saxophone player, and one was a guitar player.
Mm-hmm.
Because they was all down in the Navy band during the time of World War II. They had Tats. You know Tats?
Yeah, I knew Tats.
Well, Tats was there, down there. They had... They had them two Cadmys boys.
What were they named?
They had, uh...
Sam.
Who else? They had more rubber than Harris. Gilbert Young. You know Gilbert Young?
Yeah, I know him.
They had Gilbert Young.
Trumpet player.
They had Larry.
Herbert Leary?
Yeah, he was down in the Navy band.
What was he playing?
Yeah. And they had, uh... Who else they had down there? Uh... Uh... Know Frank Fields? You know Frank Fields?
Yeah.
Frank...
He plays in his band.
Yeah.
Plays in his band.

Frank plays in your band. Well, Frank Fields was, uh... Get-off player when he went in the Navy, but after he got in there, he started playing bass tuba. See, and that from bass tuba, then he got on the string bass. All them fellas used to be by my house every day when they was at the... when they was down in the Navy band. Every time they'd get off in the evening, they all would come by my house.
Did you know George Williams
from, uh... Yeah, George Williams. He come from Downersonville. George was, uh... George was, uh... head, uh... band man down there.
Yeah.
And little Barney Gilbert was down there, too. You know him?
No, who is he?
Oh, he's a trumpet player, too.
Oh, Vernon Gilbert.
Yeah, Barney Gilbert.
Yeah, he's kin to John Casimir, too, I think.
No, I don't believe he's no kin to John. He used to play
with John, though.

He's a mailman. That's right. He used to play with John. The mailman. That's right. He used to play with John. Yeah. That's a long time. Well, he was down in the Navy band. Practically, most of the fellows in that Navy band was right out of New Orleans. Outside George Williams, which was there, but from Dyson Root. And, uh... two trombone players. I didn't know them. They wasn't... they wasn't from here. So...
What did George Williams play?
Uh...
What did George Williams play?
George Williams? George Williams used to play trumpet and sax.
And, uh, Herbert Leary, what was he playing then?
Who that?
Leary.
He played trumpet. Yeah, he played trumpet. Yeah.
Was that his main instrument? Trumpet? Was trumpet his main instrument?
Was that his main goal? That's what he played down there.
At the Navy?
